title: Thoreau goes to the woods
hook: on 4 July 1845 he moves to Walden Pond to live deliberately and front the essential facts (Walden, chapter 2)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pascal's night of fire, and the page sewn into his coat. Your line was keep it close. Did you write your line down? Day ninety-one.

Look back at this week of ordinary saints. Socrates talking on his last day, and admitting what he didn't know. Brother Lawrence at the sink. Julian with the world in her palm. Francis walking out to a wolf. Pascal's coat with its secret page. None of them were kings. All of them paid attention. We end the week in America, on Independence Day, 1845, with a young man moving his few belongings into a tiny cabin he'd built himself beside a pond. Today's story is Thoreau goes to the woods.
screen: `A WEEK OF ORDINARY SAINTS.` → `NONE OF THEM KINGS.` → `A CABIN BY A POND, 1845.`

segments.voice: Henry David Thoreau built his cabin on the shore of Walden Pond, near Concord, Massachusetts. One room, a bed, a desk, three chairs. He wrote down exactly what it cost: twenty-eight dollars and twelve and a half cents. He lived there, as he says, two years and two months. And in his book Walden he explained why: "I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived." Deliberately. On purpose. Not by default, not by habit, not because everyone else did it that way. Now, the honest part, because it matters. Walden wasn't the wilderness. The cabin was a short walk from town. Thoreau went into Concord often, had visitors, and ate meals with his family and friends. People love to point that out, as if it spoils the story. It doesn't. The point was never to vanish. It was to strip life down far enough to see what it's made of. And then he left, and said he had several more lives to live. So the experiment wasn't the cabin. It was the question he took there: am I choosing this, or just drifting through it? You don't need a pond to ask it. You can ask it about your morning coffee, your commute, the next hour.
screen: `A CABIN BY WALDEN POND.` · `$28.12½, TWO YEARS, TWO MONTHS.` · `TO LIVE DELIBERATELY.` · `NOT A HERMIT, AN EXPERIMENT.` · then, large: `DELIBERATELY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one thing deliberately. Settle, and breathe. Choose one small thing you'll do in the next hour anyway: drinking a glass of water, walking to the door, making a call. Picture doing it on purpose, start to finish. Notice the choice to begin. Notice each part as it happens. Notice the moment you finish. Nothing extra, just awake for the whole thing. When your mind drifts to something else, notice that too, and come back. The bell holds the time.
Thoreau goes to the woods. Two years by a pond, near enough to town, to live deliberately and see what life is made of. Today's word.
screen: `THOREAU GOES TO THE WOODS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: deliberately. Today, pick one ordinary thing you usually do on autopilot, and do it on purpose, start to finish. Day ninety-one.

howItsDone: Readers of Walden often take up Thoreau's experiment in small ways: a simpler season, a walk without a phone, or asking of one habit whether it is chosen or just drifted into.
